newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: December industry output drop surprises economists.
newsitem.headline: December industry output drop surprises economists.

text.p: A two percent drop p in Yugoslavia's industrial output in the last month of 1996 surprised economists who said it was too early to say if it signified a trend or was a seasonal phenomenon.
According to official statistics released on Tuesday, year-on-year industrial output growth was reduced to 4.8 percent from 14.4 percent in November.

"Industrial output fell by two percent in December against November, which is something that is not expected because output generally picks up in the last month of the year," said Miroljub Labus, an economist with the Belgrade Economics Institute.

All branches of the economy, with the exception of energy and wood industries, marked a considerable drop in industrial activity in December, continuing the decline from November when overall output was 7.2 percent down on the previous month.
Labus said although the December drop was not yet alarming, its effect on other economic activity had to be watched.

"I don't think this is tragic. Industry was probably overinflated in the previous months. The question is how it will reflect on further activity, especially insolvency of the economy and the foreign trade deficit," Labus said.
The 1996 trade deficit topped $2.26 billion, with imports worth $4.1 billion and exports $1.85 billion.
In its latest market barometer report, the institute predicted industrial output would decline further in January which is an expected seasonal drop.
It revised its forecast for industrial output growth in the first quarter downwards, putting it at three percent above the same three-month period in 1996.
But Labus said it would take another month to determine to what extent the drop was seasonal and "to what extend it was the result of changed relations in the economy".

Production of food and energy did not significantly contribute to the rate of overall industrial output growth, which was attributed primarily to high growth rates in the metallurgy, non-metals and chemical sectors. -- Beti Bilandzic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
